newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine youth reconcile religion, sex - experts.
newsitem.headline: Philippine youth reconcile religion, sex - experts.

text.p: The co-existence of strong Catholic influences and liberal attitudes to sex has created increasing problems of disease and unwanted pregnancies in the Philippines, a population expert said on Wednesday.

More and more youngsters in the country are sexually active before marriage but attitudes about safety are affected by religious beliefs, said Satish Mehra, Manila representative of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

"We found that the young could often use religion as an excuse to suit conveniences," he said of a finding in an extensive UNFPA survey which found that 74 percent of the estimated 1.8 million young Filipino males having pre-marital sex did not use condoms.
"Some of them say using condoms is not right from the religious point of view but they don't want to consider what religion says about pre-marital sex," Mehra said.
A majority of the Philippines' 68 million people are Catholic and the church has in the past opposed condom manufacturers on the grounds that contraceptive use is against the tenets of the religion.
The UNFPA survey, presented at a seminar last weekend, was started in 1994 and polled 11,000 young adults aged between 15 and 24 from 14 provinces across the country.

"It is heartwarming to note that a majority of our youth, especially women, are not sexually active," the survey found. "By the time they are 21 years old, 82 percent of women and 55 percent of men would still be virgins."

But it cautioned that the absolute numbers of youngsters estimated to have indulged in pre-marital sex, 1.8 million men and 670,000 women, was quite large and this had increased the probabilities of associated risks like unwanted pregnancies and sex-related diseases. The survey did not say how the absolute numbers were arrived at.

The study found that social factors had varying effects on men and women with regard to the propensity for pre-marital sex. Young women who described themselves as religious were less likely to indulge in pre-marital sex but religion did not seem to affect the sexual behaviour of young men.

Peer pressure was a strong factor influencing men toward pre-marital sex, but women who were socially active were almost 50 percent less likely to have sex than those who do not mix with others, it said.

A separate paper presented at the seminar by Eliseo de Guzman of the Population Institute at the University of the Philippines, said smoking, drinking and drugs exposed youngsters to a greater likelihood of pre-marital sex.
UNFPA's Mehra said with changing social norms, a liberal attitude to sex was expected. "What we have to do is to guide the youth, so they don't make mistakes," he said.
